newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Gold demand establishes world floor price - WGC.
newsitem.headline: Gold demand establishes world floor price - WGC.

text.p: Record demand for gold is keeping a floor price on the precious metal but will not provide the catalyst to lift prices, the World Gold Council (WGC) said on Tuesday.

Gold is destined to languish near its current level of around US$340 an ounce until the big investment funds of North America and Europe reduce their hold on the market, George Milling-Stanley of WGC's economic service told analysts in Sydney.
"When they go away and play with something else, then the gold price will recover," Milling-Stanley said.
The WGC, an industry body, last week said demand for gold in the markets it served grew 17 percent in the first quarter, one of the largest increases ever recorded.
But until the funds end speculative plays in the marketplace physical demand would provide little more than a floor price of around US$340 an ounce, Milling-Stanley said.
SBC Warburg analyst Chris Baker said: "Despite high demand, the funds continue to have a strong influence on the U.S. dollar gold price."
Milling-Stanley said it was too early to tell how strong demand would be in the current quarter, although "anecdotal evidence" suggested another round of robust conditions.
Traditional scenarios whereby demand in developing economies was greatest in the first quarter and in developed markets in the fourth quarter, were starting to blur, he said.
"Seasonality is not as important as it used to be," Milling-Stanley said.
Most of the world's gold markets shared in the increase, he said.

"Continued income growth in the key consuming areas, coupled with increasing efforts to deregulate and liberalise the international trade in gold, should ensure another good performance for physical demand in 1997," Milling-Stanley said.

Analyst Alan Heap of County NatWest said he was encouraged by WGC data showing its index of local currency gold prices, which are weighted according to the size of each country's gold consumption, shows a more level trend than the U.S. dollar gold price index.
"I take that as a good sign for gold," Heap said.
In several important consuming countries, gold prices in local currencies actually moved higher during the first quarter, notably in Turkey and Germany, Milling-Stanley said.
